text:
Pilot inadvertently bumped the switch to off; no fault was found in the switch or inverters, so the cause is the pilot's action.

PILOT ERROR

The report's defect word is missing ("found of stage 1 lpt nozzle guide vanes"). The most similar labeled reports describe the same inspection finding on stage 1 LPT nozzle guide vanes, and those were labeled cracked. So the likely missing word is "cracks."

CRACKED

Passenger vaping set off the detector, so the detector worked properly and the cause was the passenger. The fitting labels are PAX ERROR or NON ISSUE. Since the passenger's action is the explicit cause, PAX ERROR is the better match.

PAX ERROR

The seat track fittings were sitting on top of the seat tracks instead of being engaged in them. That points to "NOT SEATED" or "MISINSTALLED". The fittings were not set into the tracks, which matches NOT SEATED most directly.

NOT SEATED

The report traces the flaps-locked condition to a damaged wire (# 2751-4528) between the 34CV right wing tip brake and 4008VS, which was fixed with a grade 1A repair. The open circuit found during the continuity check is a symptom of that wire damage, so the part's condition is best described as damaged.

DAMAGED

The boot was wedged between the piston and the bearing, which kept the strut compressed. "JAMMED" fits a part wedged in place better than "DISLODGED" or "MIGRATED".

JAMMED

The pack 1 valve was opening and closing on its own, without being commanded. That points to INTERMITTENT, though MALFUNCTIONED could also fit.

INTERMITTENT

Pitot cover left installed on the captain's probe. That blocks the probe, so the closest condition labels are OBSTRUCTED, BLOCKED or INSTALLED. The similar report where an obstruction was removed from the pitot tube was labeled CLOGGED, and the debris cases were labeled OBSTRUCTED. A cover is a physical obstruction rather than debris build-up, so OBSTRUCTED fits best.

OBSTRUCTED

The autopilot "would not couple," so the condition of the failed part is that it was not operating. INOPERATIVE fits this best, though FAILED is also plausible.

INOPERATIVE

The part that failed here is the door handle. It came slightly out of its seated position in flight, and pushing it back in restored the slide light. That matches NOT SEATED better than LOOSE.

NOT SEATED

The forward lav leak could not be duplicated on the ground and no leaks were found at the toilet or sink. The defect actually found was the forward sill drain float valve clogged full of mud and debris, which is the failed part's condition.

CLOGGED

Door would not open; strap was caught in latch roller area. Likely JAMMED or OBSTRUCTED. A foreign object (strap) interfered with the latch, so JAMMED fits best.

JAMMED

Drain line blockage, suspected clog — BLOCKED vs CLOGGED. A similar example with a cleared blockage was labeled BLOCKED.

BLOCKED

The report names the density controller as the failed part and says testing at Lycoming confirmed it was defective. The condition of the part itself is "failed", even though the result was a power loss.

FAILED

Door unable to close, fixed by resecuring the door. Candidate labels are MALFUNCTIONED, INOPERATIVE or UNSECURE. The fix suggests the door was loose or not secured, but the reported symptom is that the door would not close. MALFUNCTIONED or INOPERATIVE fits that symptom best, and INOPERATIVE is a common label for "unable to" reports.

INOPERATIVE

The first officer's side window was hot, bubbling and oozing fluid, with a melted plastic smell that led to a diversion. That points to a window heat failure in which the window overheated. "BURNED" and "ODOR" are possible, but "OVERHEATED" best describes the condition of the part.

OVERHEATED

Loud bangs were heard on takeoff and attributed to a compressor stall, but the engine downloads showed the actual event was a single surge on the right engine, which led to its replacement. The list has a SURGES label that matches this directly, though STALLED is how most of the similar compressor-stall reports were labeled. Because the report specifically documents a surge event as the confirmed condition, SURGES is the closer fit.

SURGES

The report describes an undocumented repair found on the frame web. That is a prior repair with no record, which points to MISREPAIRED or DISCOVERED. In similar data, "undocumented repair" findings are typically labeled MISREPAIRED.

MISREPAIRED

Of the similar reports, the bird-strike one with fan blade damage was labeled DAMAGED. This report likewise describes a bird strike followed by replacement of two fan blades, which points to blade damage.

DAMAGED

The failed part is the frangible tire burst probe. The report says it was "broken" and that hydraulic fluid was draining from it.

BROKEN

Flight attendants reported an odorous haze in the cabin, with no smoke mentioned. Both HAZE and ODOR fit the description. The report leads with the haze, so HAZE is the closer label.

HAZE

Panel departed the aircraft in flight. The closest label is INFLT SEPARATION, though MISSING (used in a similar example) was also a candidate.

INFLT SEPARATION

The insulation blanket was physically blocking the armed door lever stop, which points to INTERFERENCE. The corrective action, repositioning the blanket, might suggest OUT OF POSITION, but the stated cause is interference with the lever stop, so INTERFERENCE fits better.

INTERFERENCE

The strip itself is not damaged or malfunctioning. The issue is part number stickers left on its upper surfaces, which obscure it. The fix was cleaning, which points to a dirty or soiled surface, and DIRTY fits best.

DIRTY

Trim ran nose-up uncommanded until the clacker sounded, so this is a runaway-trim event. The closest labels are MALFUNCTIONED and UNCONTROLLABLE. The aircraft remained controllable once the autopilot was disconnected, so UNCONTROLLABLE overstates it. MALFUNCTIONED fits better.

MALFUNCTIONED

Both pilots' rudder pedals were very hard to move and needed a lot of force to free them up. They were described as "locked out in neutral". This fits STIFF or BINDS better than LOCKED; I chose STIFF.

STIFF

The report states the fault directly: "found both nose tires out of round condition." This also explains the vibration and the burning rubber smell. The odor checks found no other source, so the condition of the failed part is out of round.

OUT OF ROUND

Oil filter bypass alert in flight; filter replaced; no contamination noted. Similar cases with no contamination found are labeled FAULTY.

FAULTY

The precatch stays engaged and the fix was adjusting it, so this is an adjustment problem. A similar report with that corrective action was labeled OUT OF ADJUST.

OUT OF ADJUST

Left brake was dragging (needed right rudder and extra power, heat, smoke).

DRAGGING

Maintenance found no damage or misalignment on the door. The only defect identified was slack in the lock wire, which was then replaced. Slack in a lock wire means it was loose, so the failed part's condition is "loose" rather than the related "low tension".

LOOSE

Bungee cable caught on door stop... the cable was caught, so the door wasn't fully closed. The closest labels are "HUNG UP" or "INTERFERENCE". A cable caught on a stop is best described as interference.

INTERFERENCE

Stuck door fixed by realigning the frame; similar frame adjustments were labeled OUT OF ADJUST.

OUT OF ADJUST

Testing found no faults and the crew's problem could not be duplicated, which leaves a choice between MALFUNCTIONED and INTERMITTENT. The FMS repeatedly loaded only the back course and failed to sequence the approach correctly. That is an operational malfunction, and nothing in the report shows the problem coming and going, so MALFUNCTIONED fits better.

MALFUNCTIONED

Foreign material was found jammed in the captain's pitot probe, which caused the airspeed discrepancy. In the closest similar report, debris in a probe was labeled OBSTRUCTED, and this report fits the same pattern.

OBSTRUCTED

Air surge duct found with a hole. The closest label is DAMAGED, which matches the similar surge duct reports, though PERFORATED would also fit a hole. Those similar duct reports were labeled DAMAGED, so I'll use that.

DAMAGED

The report states that maintenance found the 100 amp hydraulic pump circuit breaker open on the right power junction box. Every subsequent check came back normal: motor amp draw, accumulator and system pressure, reservoir, fluid quantity, and multiple gear cycles. So the only actual condition identified is the breaker being open, which points to TRIPPED or OPEN.

The similar report about a popped circuit breaker was labeled FAULTED, while the one about a tripped landing gear breaker was labeled BROKEN based on the damaged wires found afterward. Here the report itself uses the word "open," and no underlying fault was found, so the direct condition is the breaker being open.

OPEN

Labels like FAULTY or FAULTED would be the default for this ram air actuator pack-light pattern, but this report states a specific finding. The left ram air inlet actuator was found "out of rig" and its rod end had a lot of slop between it and the actuator body. That points to either OUT OF RIG or EXCESS PLAY. The report names "out of rig" first and explicitly, so OUT OF RIG is the closest match.

OUT OF RIG

The handle cover was installed in the incorrect position, so the slide could not be armed with the cover closed. That points to an installation error, which fits MISINSTALLED better than OUT OF POSITION.

MISINSTALLED

The part that failed is the #1 brake. It was dragging, which caused it to overheat, melt the fuse plug and deflate both tires. "Dragging" is the core condition and is on the list, though "OVERHEATED" would also be defensible.

DRAGGING

Red lights flashing at all four main cabin doors, and they had stopped flashing by the time the item was deferred. This matches the two earlier ship 3236 reports of flashing door/exit lights that could not be reproduced, which were labeled INTERMITTENT.

INTERMITTENT

Brake assembly seized, so the aircraft could not move under power. The closest label is LOCKED or SEIZED; "seized" is not on the list, so the choice is among STUCK, LOCKED and FROZEN. "Seized" most commonly maps to STUCK.

STUCK

The report's final finding is that the EPR P4.95 tube was found loose at the 3 o'clock position, and then that the tube was damaged. "Loose" is the condition that was found first and the one tied to the troubleshooting guidance, which asked mechanics to check for cracked, broken or loose tubes. "Damaged" is the competing choice, but the looseness looks like the primary condition.

LOOSE

The root cause was the MEL procedure not being accomplished properly, which is a maintenance error. The skin air outlet valve was reinstated with no part defect found.

MECHANIC ERROR

Similar case: the gen disconnect caution light on start run-up was labeled ILLUMINATED, and this report follows the same pattern of a caution light coming on during run-up. OVERSPEED is a possibility, but the light was likely false, since the tach box was replaced.

ILLUMINATED

Fluttering flight controls describe an oscillating or vibrating condition. Of the two candidate labels, OSCILLATES and VIBRATES, VIBRATES fits flutter best.

VIBRATES

Gauges showed 1/4 fuel when the tanks were actually empty, so the fault is the fuel gauges reading higher than the true quantity.

READS HIGH

Visible haze in the aft galley; options are SMOKE or HAZE. The "-smke-" tag marks this as a smoke event, so SMOKE fits best.

SMOKE

Uncommanded flap extension at FL380, followed by fluctuation; the fix was replacing the flap power supply and the RH flap position transmitter, both described as faulty. The candidates are "MALFUNCTIONED" or "FAULTY". Since the report repeatedly says "removed faulty", the label is FAULTY.

FAULTY

The closest match is the near-identical report labeled FAULTED, but that label likely came from details in its supplemental text, which is truncated here. This report is still open and describes only the fuel imbalance. Similar open imbalance reports were labeled OUT OF BALANCE.

OUT OF BALANCE

Grit from the runway coated the brakes and caused the grabbing, so the condition is contamination.

CONTAMINATED

Troubleshooting found no faults and no defects, but a cabin altitude caution message was received in flight. Similar reports with this pattern were labeled WARNING MESSAGE.

WARNING MESSAGE

The root cause found was the door closeouts being misaligned, which made the door bind. The dry pins were a secondary finding, so the condition is misalignment rather than lack of lube.

MISALIGNED

Tank 1 quantity falsely dropping to 0 and the loss of fuel flow indications cleared on their own after a few minutes, so the fault was intermittent. The closest similar reports, where the fuel conditioning unit was replaced, are labeled FAULTED. Of the available labels, a transient indication fault with no duplication fits INTERMITTENT, but following the similar reports' convention points to FAULTED.

FAULTED

Here the end cap did not match up with the newly installed leading edge skin. That points to a fit or alignment problem, likely the wrong part or a mismanufactured one. The options are MISALIGNED, OUT OF ALIGNMENT, WRONG PART and IMPROPER PART. "Did not match up" reads most naturally as an alignment issue, and the part was replaced. I'll go with MISALIGNED.

MISALIGNED

Suspected blown tire, nose wheel replaced. The closest example (possible tire damage, wheel replaced) was labeled DAMAGED. The crew suspected a blown tire, but the report doesn't confirm a burst. The shaking points toward VIBRATES, but the part that was replaced is the tire. I'll pick DAMAGED.

DAMAGED

Inspection found the 13WN microswitch sticky with CPC anti-corrosion compound and it was cleaned. The cause was a foreign substance on the switch, which points to CONTAMINATED. STICKING was the main alternative, but the report frames the problem as compound coating the switch rather than a mechanical sticking fault.

CONTAMINATED

The report says the sensor ground GD614AC was found out of tolerance. That matches the similar example where an S168 terminal reading out of tolerance was labeled OUT OF TOLERANCE.

OUT OF TOLERANCE

Under the labeling scheme, the condition to classify is the found defect on the #100 ICU, not the cockpit message. The report says the valve was surging while deploying the thrust reversers, with a small leak noted as secondary evidence. The surging is the stated malfunction, so SURGES fits best. LEAKING and WARNING MESSAGE were the alternatives considered.

SURGES
